artboards.title: Today: Your evening on the living room TV
A: the wall, from the sofa
C: the room, over the picture

annotations.text:
WHY THIS EXISTS

19 November 2026: a Hub Plus (an N150 mini PC) went on the living room TV over HDMI, and the box is staying in the room. The panel already draws well at 1920x1080. It cannot be used from the sofa: the remote's arrows and OK do nothing, nothing is lit to say where you are, the smallest words are 14px at three meters, and dimming is a drag and More is a hold on glass.

What a remote gives us: four arrows, OK, Back and Home, and on most TV remotes four colored buttons. They reach the hub three ways: the TV's own remote over HDMI-CEC (this box has no CEC, so a USB adapter, whose driver is in the kernel the image now ships), any USB or Bluetooth remote that types arrow keys, and later a remote of our own. Every one of them can tell a press from a hold.

What this does not change: films stay as design/media decided (D), the wall and the phone stay as they are, and the tab row stays three.

THE SAME IN EVERY DIRECTION

ONLY ON A TV. Worked out the way the wall's keyboard is (onWall in keys.ts): a screen plugged into the hub, or a browser that says it is a TV. A phone and the wall never see any of this.

THE KEYS. The arrows move the highlight to the nearest thing that way. OK does what a tap does, holding OK does what a hold does, and Back goes back. Each board here answers to a keyboard the same way: arrows, Enter for OK, Escape for Back.

THE HIGHLIGHT IS LIGHT. A lamp-colored rim and a small lift, never a thin outline, and one line beside it says in words what OK will do here.

NOTHING VANISHES UNDER THE HIGHLIGHT. A light turned off from the sofa stays where it was, drained, exactly as on the wall (the done map in store.ts).

SIZED FOR THE SOFA. Nothing a person must read is under 22px, and everything sits inside the 5% a TV may crop from its edges.

TODAY. The shipped panel on the mock house at 7:40 PM, in a 1920x1080 browser, which is what the hub's Chromium hands a 1080p TV. It is the wall's evening with more room around it. Pressed with a keyboard, the arrows and Enter change nothing; Tab reaches a face in the top corner first.

A — THE WALL, FROM THE SOFA. The TV gets exactly the wall: the hub's browser zooms so the page is the wall's 1440 wide, which makes everything a third bigger, and a lamp-colored rim walks from card to card with the arrows. Under the lit card, one line: OK turns it off, hold OK for brightness and color. The dock is the last row, reached with Down.

FOR: there is no second layout. Every screen and sheet the wall has works from the sofa on the first day, and whatever the wall gains, the TV gains.

AGAINST: it is still a wall. Its smallest words are 19px, under the sofa's 22. The row of cards runs off the right edge, as it does on the wall, and a remote has to walk there. Dimming is two steps (hold OK, then the arrows in the sheet), which is the thing done most from a sofa.

B — ROWS, FROM THE SOFA. The TV opens on the room it is in, because that is where the person holding the remote is. Rows go down the screen: what is in this room, its scenes, the other rooms, the cameras. Up and Down move between rows, and the lit row rides to the top while the ones above slide away. OK does the tap, holding OK does the hold, and the line at the foot says which.

FOR: it is the grammar every TV already teaches, so nobody learns anything. Everything in the house is a few presses away, and every word is sized for the sofa.

AGAINST: it is a second layout to keep in step with the wall's, and it gives up the wall's composed evening for rows. Using it means leaving whatever is on the TV.

C — THE ROOM, OVER THE PICTURE. The TV stays a TV. OK (or Home) brings this room up over whatever the hub is showing, in one band along the foot, and Back puts it away; the film keeps playing behind it. Left and Right move along the room's things. Up and Down are the level itself: brighter or dimmer, warmer or cooler, the blinds up or down, one press each, with the meter on the lit card. The four colored buttons start the room's four scenes without opening anything, and the band says which color is which.

FOR: dimming from the sofa is one press, not a hold and a sheet. The house is something you glance at over the film, not a place you go. The colored buttons finally do something.

AGAINST: only this room is first-class; the rest of the house is behind Other rooms. It can draw over the picture only when the hub is what is on. Over the TV's own apps it has to switch the TV to the hub, which takes the film away and needs CEC. Because Up and Down are the level, the band is one row, by design.

DECIDED 19 NOVEMBER 2026 -- B, WITH C'S BAND OVER A FILM

The TV opens on B: its own room first, then scenes, the other rooms and the cameras, in rows. While the hub is playing a film, OK or Home brings C's band up over it instead of leaving the film: this room's things along the foot, Up and Down as the level, the colored buttons as the room's scenes, Back to put it away. A is kept on the page beside this one, with its case.

NOT CHOSEN

The wall zoomed a third is one layout to keep, but its smallest words stay under the sofa's 22px and dimming stays two steps. B gives the sofa its own sizes, and C's band gives it one-press dimming over a film.
